# Power {#sec-power}

The power block is CPAT's techno-economic ("engineer") power model. Every year it works out how much electricity the
economy needs, which plants generate it, which plants retire, what is built to replace them, what it all costs and
what electricity users pay.

It is the largest block of the model and the one where most of the sector's policy effects arise: a carbon price
changes the cost of each generation type, which changes dispatch and investment, which changes the generation mix,
emissions, the cost of supply and, a year later, electricity prices and demand.

The methodology describes the power models in
[section 3.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#power-sector-models): power prices and generation costs
in [3.4.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PowerPrices), the engineer model in
[3.4.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-EngineerModel), and the data in
[3.4.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PowerDataSources). The methodology also has an
elasticity-based power model ([3.4.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-ElasticityModel)) and,
for it, the "old" generation costs of
[Appendix C](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#power-generation-costs). Excel-AI and CPAT Python
implement the engineer model only; the elasticity model is not part of this book. (The methodology's corrections of
2026-10-31 to these two parts, DOC5 and DOC15, therefore have no counterpart here; the corrections that concern the
engineer model are linked in the sections below:
[corrections](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/08_Corrections.html#corrections-of-2026-10-31).)

The chapter follows the order of the calculation:

| Section | What it computes | Legacy sub-table |

| [Order of the calculation](#sec-pw-order) | Which quantity of which year feeds which | - |
| [Electricity demand](#sec-pw-demand) | Demand by subsector, required generation | H |
| [Generation costs](#sec-pw-costs) | Inputs of the scenario, fixed, levelised and variable costs, total costs, memos | A, B, C, D, E, F |
| [Dispatch](#sec-pw-dispatch) | Generation by type, fuel use, CO2 | I |
| [Capacity and retirement](#sec-pw-capacity) | Capacity, retirement, early coal retirement, capacity needed | K |
| [Investment](#sec-pw-investment) | New capacity by type and its cost | L |
| [Storage](#sec-pw-storage) | Systems integration cost of renewables | J |
| [End-user prices](#sec-pw-prices) | Residential and industrial electricity prices, subsidies | G |
| [Power revenues](#sec-pw-revenues) | Revenue by user group and by generation type | G4, M |
| [Coal implicit cost](#sec-pw-coalic) | The calibrated extra cost of coal | D3 |

## The power block at a glance {#sec-pw-glance}

### Generation types {#sec-pw-types}

The model has nine generation types. Two of them, coal and gas, are dispatched by cost. The other seven run at their
capacity factor whenever they exist.

| Type $f$ | Code | Dispatch | Variable renewable (VRE) | Fuel price used | Legacy code |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coal | `coa` | by cost (CG) | no | coal for power (`coa.pow`) | `coa` |
| Natural gas | `nga` | by cost (CG) | no | gas for power (`nga.pow`) | `nga` |
| Oil | `oop` | fixed output | no | other oil products (`oop.all`) | `oil` |
| Nuclear | `nuc` | fixed output | no | none (fixed fuel cost) | `nuc` |
| Wind | `wnd` | fixed output | yes | none | `wnd` |
| Solar | `sol` | fixed output | yes | none | `sol` |
| Hydro | `hyd` | fixed output | no | none | `hyd` |
| Other renewables | `ore` | fixed output | yes | none | `ore` |
| Biomass | `bio` | fixed output | no | biomass (`bio.all`) | `bio` |

$CG = \{\text{coal}, \text{gas}\}$ is the set of dispatchable types. The VRE set is wind, solar and other renewables:
it sets the storage cost ([Storage](#sec-pw-storage)). Oil generation sums the energy-balance fuels other oil
products, gasoline, diesel, kerosene, LPG and jet fuel.

### Notation {#sec-pw-notation}

The chapter uses the notation of the methodology where it has a symbol, and the symbol of the equation list
(@sec-eqlist) otherwise.

- **Indices.** Generation type $f$; user group $g \in \{\text{res}, \text{ind}\}$ (residential, industry); demand
  group $d \in \{\text{tra}, \text{res}, \text{ind}, \text{srv}\}$ (transport, residential, industry, services);
  subsector $s$; year $t$. Every equation holds for each scenario $o$ and country $c$; these two indices are omitted.
  A value of the baseline in the same year carries the superscript $B$.
- **Years.** $t_0$ is the base year (first year of calculations, 2022), $L$ the last historical price year (2024 for
  the current data), $T = 2041$ the last model year.
- **Units.** Generation and capacity in MW (generation as MWy, i.e. average MW over the year); demand in ktoe; costs
  in real US dollars of the results year (2026) per kWh (USD/kWh); capital costs in USD/kW; money flows in USD million.
- **Constants.** $H = 8{,}760$ hours per year; $\theta_e = 0.0036$ GJ per kWh; 8.76 million kWh per MWy (`MWyMkWh`);
  $\theta_g = 11.63$ GWh per ktoe (`KtoeGWh`); 0.041868 PJ per ktoe.
- **Minimum cost.** $c_{min}$ = `MinPostSubsidyPowerPrice` (default 0.01 USD/kWh) is the floor on costs that
  enter a ratio (dispatch and investment logits) and on end-user prices.

The CPAT variable code of each quantity is given in code font (`cap`, `tic`, ...): it is the row code of Excel-AI and
the variable of CPAT Python.

### Inputs by scenario {#sec-pw-inputs-by-scenario}

Every power input of the scenario sheet is read in the scenario's own column. This covers capacity-factor and
efficiency bounds, WACC options, discounted lifetimes, investment permissions and start years, scale-up and
retirement rates, the early-retirement factor, the capex decline scenario, storage, PPAs, renewable subsidies,
rebates and excises. The sub-table A0 ([Inputs of the scenario](#sec-pw-a0)) applies them to the power data of the
country.

Scenario 1 is the baseline of every scenario. A technical input (logit constants, WACC, capacity-factor bounds,
storage, cost decline) changed in a policy scenario therefore changes that scenario only, and its difference from
scenario 1 mixes the input change with the policy. Technical inputs are not usually changed across scenarios.

Not read, because the model has no such feature: `CostBreakdownYear` (the cost breakdown is computed for every year
instead), `ElasticityModel`, `PowGenCostsOldNew`, `UseElasticityModelPowerDemandInEngineerModel`. The final deficit
to gas ([Investment](#sec-pw-deficit-gas)) is a global setting, not a scenario input.

### Links with the rest of the model {#sec-pw-links}

| From / to | What flows | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Prices (@sec-prices) to power | Fuel prices before new policies of coal and gas for power, oil, biomass; existing carbon pricing | [Variable costs](#sec-pw-vc) |
| Policies (@sec-model-overview) to power | Carbon tax and ETS rates of power, fuel coverage, shadow price, fuel price reform, carbon price path | [Variable costs](#sec-pw-vc), [Prices](#sec-pw-prices) |
| GDP (@sec-fiscal) to power | GDP growth after the feedback, of the year | [Demand](#sec-pw-demand) |
| Road transport (@sec-transport) to power | Road electricity demand, where the road engineer model is on | [Demand](#sec-pw-demand) |
| Power to fuel totals (@sec-demand) | Generation fuel use of coal, gas, oil and biomass (nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables use no fuel) | [Dispatch](#sec-pw-dispatch) |
| Power to emissions (@sec-emissions) | Power CO2 by fuel, and as ETS sector power | [Dispatch](#sec-pw-dispatch) |
| Power to revenues (@sec-fiscal) | Taxes and subsidies on generation fuels, existing carbon pricing, electricity VAT and subsidy gap, new policies | [Power revenues](#sec-pw-revenues) |
| Power to road transport (@sec-transport) | Electricity prices of last year | [Prices](#sec-pw-prices) |

Power demand follows its own elasticities. Sector policies (carbon tax, ETS, feebates, fuel price reform) act on the
fuel blocks; they reach power demand only through the electricity price. Electricity demand by sector is a memo in the
sector blocks, not part of the fuel totals, so nothing is counted twice.

Power CO2 enters the CO2 totals by fuel and as the ETS sector power, so an ETS covering power sees it, and the
baseline CO2 data include it. Existing carbon pricing changes the variable cost before new policies
([Variable costs](#sec-pw-vc)).

## Order of the calculation within a year and across years {#sec-pw-order}

The power block runs once per year, inside the year loop, after the GDP level of the year and before fuel use. A few
rows that depend only on prices and policies are computed for all years before the loop. Everything else is computed
year by year, and the chain is free of circular references because two links are lagged by one year.

The methodology summarises the algorithm in
[section 3.4.2.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#overview-2).

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 5
flowchart TD
  H["H demand, required generation"] --> I["K1, I capacity of the year, dispatch"]
  I --> J["J storage: VRE share, storage cost"]
  J --> E["B, C, E costs: fixed, levelised, average"]
  E --> K["K retirement, early coal, capacity needed"]
  E -. "next year" .-> G["G prices"]
  K --> L["L investment"]
  L -. "next year: capacity" .-> I
  G -. "next year" .-> H
```

Solid arrows run within year $t$; dotted arrows carry a value of year $t$ into year $t+1$: investment becomes
capacity, the average generation cost becomes the supply cost of next year's prices, and the prices drive next year's
demand.

Within year $t$ the order is:

1. **Demand (H).** Electricity demand of year $t$ from last year's demand, this year's GDP growth and the change in
   last year's electricity prices. Required generation follows.
2. **Capacity (K1).** Capacity of year $t$ = capacity of $t-1$ less retirement of $t-1$ plus investment of $t-1$.
   Capacity bought in year $t$ is available in $t+1$.
3. **Dispatch (I).** Generation by type from capacity, required generation and the variable costs of year $t$.
4. **Storage (J).** The VRE share of generation sets the marginal storage cost of year $t$.
5. **Costs (B, C, E).** Fixed costs of the existing stock (vintages) and of new plants; the average generation cost
   and the average policy cost per kWh.
6. **Prices (G).** End-user prices of year $t$ use the average generation cost of $t-1$.
7. **Retirement (K).** Retirement of year $t$, including early coal retirement, which compares the coal variable cost
   with the wind and solar investment costs of year $t$.
8. **Investment (L).** Investment of year $t$ fills the gap between expected requirement and capacity after
   retirement, allocated by a logit over the levelised costs of year $t$. Its share in the stock, $\Phi$, feeds the
   vintage averages of $t+1$.
9. **Revenues (M).** Power revenues of year $t$.

The levelised variable cost of year $t$ averages the variable cost from $t$ to the end of the horizon. Variable costs
depend only on prices and policies, not on the generation mix, so it is computed before the year loop, backwards from
the last year.

The table lists every link of the block with the rest of the model and how the loop is broken.

| # | From | To | What flows | How the loop is broken |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I1 | Fuel prices (coal and gas for power, oil, biomass) | D variable costs | Fuel price before new policies | One way |
| I2 | Policies (carbon price, ETS power coverage, fuel price reform) | D policy cost; G end-user prices; revenues | Carbon cost per kWh by type | One way |
| I3 | Generation mix (dispatch I, investment L) | E average generation cost; J storage (via the VRE share) | Generation shares by type | Dispatch uses current variable costs, which do not depend on the average cost; prices use last year's average cost (I5) |
| I4 | Investment (L) | B vintage averages of capex and storage cost | New investment as a share of remaining capacity $\Phi$ | B uses last year's $\Phi$ |
| I5 | E average generation cost | G end-user prices | Supply cost = average generation cost + transmission | **Lagged one year**: the price in $t$ uses the cost of $t-1$ |
| I6 | G end-user prices | Demand, generation, I3 | Residential and industrial prices | Through I5's lag; demand uses last year's prices, by demand group |
| I7 | J storage | B (vintage storage cost) and C (levelised cost, for investment) | Marginal storage cost of wind, solar, other renewables | Uses the current VRE share from dispatch |
| I8 | C levelised costs, D levelised variable costs | Investment logit; switching carbon prices | Levelised investment cost by type | Investment only: not in end-user prices |
| I9 | G and M revenues | Revenue totals | USD million | One way |

Two consequences shape the design:

1. **End-user prices depend on generation costs only through the weighted average** (E) and the transmission
   add-on. Variable, amortised and storage costs matter for prices only as far as they enter that average.
2. **The systems cost of renewables is an interaction inside the block.** The VRE share sets the marginal storage
   cost, which enters the cost of wind, solar and other renewables twice: *amortised*, through vintages, in the cost
   of the existing stock (B), which reaches end-user prices; and *levelised*, in the cost of new plants (C), which
   drives investment. A scenario that adds renewables therefore raises their storage cost per kWh, which feeds back
   into the average generation cost and, a year later, into prices.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: the power block"}
```
# before the year loop (power.prepare)
for t in years:
    settings of the scenario: cfu, nuu, wac, dlf, perm, start, rate, rr, erf, ppa, rns, rbs, exs
    for f in types:
        cax[f,t] = cax0[f] * tcf[f,t]
        tvc[f,t] = vbc[f,t] + xac[f,t] + shk[f,t] + reb[t]      # variable cost incl. policies
for f in types:                                                   # backwards from the last year
    lvc[f,:] = discounted average of tvc[f, t..2041]

# the year loop (power.step), t = 2022 .. 2041
for t in years:
    dem, req          = demand(rp[:, t-1], gdp growth[t])          # H
    cap[:, t]         = cap[:, t-1] - ret[:, t-1] + nim[:, t-1]     # K1
    gen, shr, pe, co2 = dispatch(cap, req, tvc[:, t])               # I
    vre, msc          = storage(shr)                                 # J
    fix, lfx, gnc     = costs(phi[:, t-1], msc)                      # B, C, E
    gncav, ccpav, tic = averages(shr), lfx + lvc                     # E
    rp                = prices(gncav[t-1], ccpav)                    # G (supply cost lagged)
    ret, early        = retirement(cap, tvc, tic)                    # K
    nim, phi          = investment(req, cap, ret, tic)               # L
    revenues                                                         # G4, M
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check: properties that hold in every run"}
These properties are tested on every build (`check_report`, check section 5d), in the baseline and in every policy
scenario:

- generation = required generation (where capacity allows);
- the capacity balance holds: $cap_t = cap_{t-1} - ret_{t-1} + inv_{t-1}$;
- investment is at most the capacity needed (scale-up limits can leave part unplaced);
- the supply cost lag holds: the price of $t$ uses the cost of $t-1$;
- a carbon price raises the VRE share and lowers power CO2, as checked in the test scenarios; it is not a property of
  every year (in Egypt's scenario 2 the VRE share is below the baseline's from 2030, see [Storage](#sec-pw-storage));
- the memo lines equal power demand by subsector and add up by sector and in total;
- fuel use, revenue and CO2 totals with power equal the Python reference; with non-zero existing carbon pricing test
  data, the power variable cost, revenues by type and totals match too; check rows confirm that the totals equal
  their sector, power and fuel parts.

Further checks:

- **Method = legacy.** The Python reference of the method, fed with the cached legacy inputs and the bugs switched on,
  reproduces 208 legacy rows of the baseline and the carbon-tax run.
- **Workbook = Python reference.** With all bugs fixed and the model's inputs, the workbook matches the Python
  reference for every power row, in every scenario test.
- **Planned retirement.** With the switch on for gas and oil and test data, the workbook matches the Python reference,
  and retirement equals the data.
- **Power features.** One test scenario per feature: `MaximumGasCF` and long-term storage; the power inputs of the
  scenario (two scenarios with many inputs changed, including WACC options, capacity-factor and efficiency bounds,
  permits, scale-up categories, decline options, storage, logit constants, pass-through, spot prices); PPAs;
  renewable subsidies; the rebate; the electricity excise and the manual excise; the final deficit to gas with tight
  scale-up limits. Each matches the Python reference.
- **CPAT Python = Excel-AI.** Every output code of Excel-AI's stored values for Egypt, scenarios 1 and 2, 2022-2041,
  matches within 1e-9.
:::

## Electricity demand and required generation {#sec-pw-demand}

Electricity demand grows with GDP, falls with efficiency gains and responds to the electricity price of the previous
year. It is computed for 15 subsectors, grouped into four demand groups that share elasticities and a price. Required
generation adds what the grid needs on top of final demand: net exports, losses, own use and statistical differences.

The methodology describes this in
[section 3.4.2.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#power-demand), with the general fuel-demand
equation of [section 3.3.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-FuelConsumptionDynamics). The model
follows the corrected form: the GDP elasticity is $\epsilon_Y$, adjusted for the income level
([corrections, DOC4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/08_Corrections.html#corrections-of-2026-10-31)).

### Demand groups and the demand price {#sec-pw-demand-price}

Each subsector belongs to one demand group. The group's price is a blend of last year's residential and industrial
end-user prices:

$$
\bar{p}_{d,t} = w_d\, p^T_{res,t-1} + (1 - w_d)\, p^T_{ind,t-1}
$$ {#eq-pw-demand-price}

where

- $\bar{p}_{d,t}$ is the electricity price seen by demand group $d$ in year $t$ (USD/kWh; `pdem`);
- $p^T_{g,t-1}$ is the end-user price of user group $g$ of the previous year (USD/kWh; `rp`,
  [End-user prices](#sec-pw-prices));
- $w_d$ is the weight of the residential price: 0.5 for transport, 1 for residential, 0 for industry and services.

In the base year the price is that of the year before (2021) from the price data. Using last year's price is what
keeps demand free of a circular reference with this year's price (link I6).

| Demand group $d$ | Subsectors $s$ | Weight $w_d$ |
|---|---|---|
| Transport (`tra`) | road, rail, domestic aviation, domestic navigation | 0.5 |
| Residential (`res`) | residential | 1 |
| Industry (`ind`) | food and forestry, mining and chemicals, iron and steel, non-ferrous metals, machinery, cement, other manufacturing, construction, other energy use | 0 |
| Services (`srv`) | services | 0 |

### The demand multiple {#sec-pw-demand-multiple}

Demand grows each year by a multiple of four factors: efficiency, GDP, price and an optional shock. It is built in two
steps.

The efficiency multiple combines the autonomous efficiency gain of the group and any additional efficiency gain of the
scenario:

$$
a_{d} = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_d + \alpha^{+}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U,d}}
$$ {#eq-pw-aeef}

The demand multiple of year $t$ is then

$$
M_{d,t} = a_{d}\,
\left(1 + \gamma_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y,d}\, inc_t}\,
\left(\frac{\bar{p}_{d,t}}{\bar{p}_{d,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U,d} + \epsilon_{F,d} + \epsilon_{U,d}\epsilon_{F,d}}\,
\left(1 + \Psi_t\, \sigma\, \psi\right)
$$ {#eq-pw-mult}

where

- $a_d$ is the efficiency multiple (`aeef`);
- $\alpha_d$ is the autonomous annual efficiency improvement of electricity in group $d$ (share per year) and
  $\alpha^{+}$ the additional efficiency gain of the scenario (`AdditionalEfficiencyPower`, default 0);
- $\epsilon_{Y,d}$, $\epsilon_{U,d}$, $\epsilon_{F,d}$ are the income, usage and efficiency elasticities of electricity
  demand of the group (the country's elasticities, @sec-demand);
- $\gamma_t$ is real GDP growth of year $t$ after the GDP feedback (`gdp.pos.pct`, @sec-fiscal);
- $inc_t$ is the income factor on the GDP elasticity (`inc.ela.adj`; [Year paths](#sec-pw-data-paths)), 1 if
  `IncElAdj` is not Yes;
- $\Psi_t$ is the exogenous demand shock (`shock`): the legacy calibration for 2023 and 2024, 0 in other years;
- $\sigma$ is the global switch that applies the shock (Excel-AI Settings C19, on by default) and $\psi$ the scenario
  input `EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor`.

The multiple is 1 in the base year. The price term uses the total price elasticity
$\epsilon_{U} + \epsilon_{F} + \epsilon_{U}\epsilon_{F}$, the product of the usage and efficiency responses. This is
the methodology's equation with its two price terms combined:
$(p_t/p_{t-1})^{\epsilon_U}\,(p_t/p_{t-1})^{\epsilon_F(1+\epsilon_U)}$. The equation list has it as
([M4.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-1)).

### Demand by subsector {#sec-pw-demand-subsector}

Each subsector's demand grows with the multiple of its group:

$$
E_{s,t} = E_{s,t-1}\, M_{d(s),t}, \qquad E_{s,t_0} = \text{base-year data}
$$ {#eq-pw-demand}

where $E_{s,t}$ is electricity demand of subsector $s$ (ktoe; `dem`) and $d(s)$ its demand group. Total demand is
$E_t = \sum_s E_{s,t}$ (`demtot`), and demand by group (`demg`) is a memo.

- **Base year.** Demand by subsector comes from the energy balance (flow `ecy` of the subsector's balance flow) or,
  if `BalancesOrConsumption` is Consumption, from the CPAT energy consumption data.
- **Road.** Where the road engineer model is on (@sec-transport), road electricity demand is taken from it instead
  of the multiple.
- **Memo lines.** Electricity demand by subsector, by sector and in total is shown in the sector blocks; it is not
  part of the fuel totals.

### Required generation {#sec-pw-required}

Generation must cover final demand plus net exports, transmission and distribution losses, statistical differences
and transfers, and the energy industry's own use. The model holds each of these at its base-year share of final
demand:

$$
req_t = \rho\, E_t, \qquad
\rho = \left(1 + s_{nxp} + s_{tsd} + s_{eou} + s_{add}\right) \frac{\theta_g \cdot 1000}{H}
$$ {#eq-pw-req}

where

- $req_t$ is required generation (MWy; `req`);
- $\rho$ is MWy of generation per ktoe of final demand (`req_factor`; $\theta_g \cdot 1000/H = 1.3276$ MWy per ktoe);
- $s_{nxp}$, $s_{tsd}$, $s_{eou}$ are the base-year shares of net exports, of transmission, distribution and
  statistical differences, and of own use in final electricity demand; $s_{add}$ is the residual that makes the sum
  equal base-year generation over base-year demand ([Parameters](#sec-pw-data-params)).

In the base year, required generation is actual generation, $req_{t_0} = \sum_f gen_{f,t_0}$. Because
$1 + s_{nxp} + s_{tsd} + s_{eou} + s_{add}$ is base-year generation over base-year demand, the two definitions agree in
the base year. The equation list has this as ([M4.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-2)).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: electricity demand and required generation"}
```
for t in years:
    for d in ['tra', 'res', 'ind', 'srv']:
        if t == base_year:
            pdem[d,t] = wres[d] * rp2021['res'] + (1 - wres[d]) * rp2021['ind']
            mult[d,t] = 1
        else:
            pdem[d,t] = wres[d] * rp['res',t-1] + (1 - wres[d]) * rp['ind',t-1]
            aeef[d]   = (1 / (1 + alpha[d] + AdditionalEfficiencyPower)) ** (1 + eps_u[d])
            mult[d,t] = (aeef[d] * (1 + gdp_growth[t]) ** (eps_y[d] * inc_ela_adj[t])
                         * (pdem[d,t] / pdem[d,t-1]) ** (eps_u[d] + eps_f[d] + eps_u[d] * eps_f[d])
                         * (1 + shock[t] * apply_shock * EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor))
    for s in subsectors:
        if t == base_year:            dem[s,t] = dem0[s]                     # Balances or EnergyCons
        elif s == 'rod' and road_engineer_model_on:  dem[s,t] = road_electricity[t]
        else:                         dem[s,t] = dem[s,t-1] * mult[group[s],t]
    demtot[t] = sum(dem[s,t] for s in subsectors)
    req[t] = sum(gen0[f] for f in types) if t == base_year else demtot[t] * req_factor
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 3, sub-table H: rows `pdem`, `aeef`, `mult` (LAMBDA `DEMANDMULT` in 2041),
  `dem`, `demg`, `demtot`, `req` (Formulas.md E384-E390). Elasticities and weights on Inputs rows 231-234 (demand
  groups), base-year demand on Inputs (subsectors), the MWy per ktoe factor on Inputs B261. Scenario inputs
  `AdditionalEfficiencyPower`, `IncElAdj`, `EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor`; Settings C19 for the shock.
- **CPAT Python:** `power.step()`, block "demand" (EQ-M4.1, EQ-M4.2); data in `power_data.demand_groups()`,
  `demand_subsectors()`, `system_params()` (`req_factor`).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT: demand"}
- **L1 (fixed).** Legacy grows services electricity demand with the industrial multiple after 2023; the model uses the
  services multiple in every year.
- **L2 (fixed).** Legacy raises the autonomous efficiency term to the power of the efficiency elasticity; the model
  uses the usage elasticity, $1 + \epsilon_U$, as the methodology.
- **L3 (fixed).** Legacy applies the income factor on the GDP elasticity twice and anchors it to 2023; the model
  applies it once.
- **L95.** In legacy the efficiency increment of power demand sits on the net-exports row (legacy bug register).
- **LD21, LD24 (same as legacy).** The 2023-2024 shock is applied as legacy, to fuels and power alike (Settings C19,
  on by default; issue I92). The methodology calls it a Covid adjustment calibrated for 2020-2021
  ([section 3.3.4.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-CalibrationCovid)); the model uses
  legacy's stored shocks for 2023 and 2024 (GHGs data, [Year paths](#sec-pw-data-paths)).
- **LD25.** Sector policies act on power demand only through the price; electricity demand is a memo line in the
  sector blocks and section 11.
- **LD27.** Road electricity comes from the road engineer model where it is on; otherwise it grows with the transport
  multiple, as legacy.
- **Not built.** The option to take power demand from the elasticity model
  (`UseElasticityModelPowerDemandInEngineerModel`).
:::

## Generation costs {#sec-pw-costs}

What a kWh costs depends on the question asked. The methodology therefore uses four cost concepts
([section 3.4.1.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#power-generation-cost-and-price-concepts)), and
the model computes each of them by generation type:

| Concept | Used for | Model quantity | Methodology |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Current variable cost | Dispatch between coal and gas; early coal retirement | $tvc_{f,t}$ (`tvc`) | [3.4.1.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-1-current-variable-costs) |
| 2. Levelised (forward-looking) cost | Investment | $tic_{f,t}$ (`tic`) | [3.4.1.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-2-levelized-costs-of-generation-forward-looking) |
| 3. Cost-recovery generation cost | Average cost of supply, and so prices | $gnc_{f,t}$ (`gnc`), $gnc^{av}_t$ (`gncav`) | [3.4.1.6](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-3-cost-recovery-estimated-total-cost-of-generation) |
| 4. End-user price | Demand, revenues, distribution | $p^T_{g,t}$ (`rp`) | [3.4.1.7](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-4-end-user-prices); [End-user prices](#sec-pw-prices) |

The first three are built from a few blocks, each computed once: the inputs of the scenario (A0), the capital cost
path, the amortised fixed cost of the existing stock (B), the levelised fixed cost of new plants (C) and the current
variable cost (D). Their combinations are the total costs (E). Memo rows (F) report switching carbon prices and a cost
breakdown.

### Inputs of the scenario {#sec-pw-a0}

Sub-table A0 applies the power inputs of the scenario to the power data of the country
([Power data](#sec-pw-data)). The results are constant over the years of a scenario.

**Capacity factor.** The actual base-year capacity factor is used when it lies strictly inside the bounds of the
scenario; otherwise the value of the studies is used:

$$
cf_f = \begin{cases} cf^{a}_f & \text{if } cf^{lo}_f < cf^{a}_f < cf^{hi} \\ cf^{s}_f & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pw-cf}

where $cf^a_f$ is base-year generation over base-year installed capacity, $cf^s_f$ the studies value, $cf^{lo}_f$ =
`CFOverrideIfBelowWndSol` (default 0.1) for wind and solar and `CFOverrideIfBelowFosOth` (0.01) for the others, and
$cf^{hi}$ = `CFOverrideIfAbove` (1). Code `cfu`.

**Efficiency.** The actual efficiency (base-year output over input) is used unless it is below
`MinimumThermalEfficiency` (default 0.1) or there is no input; then the studies value is used. Wind, solar, hydro and
other renewables have efficiency 1 by convention. Code $\nu_f$, `nuu`.

**WACC.** The option `WACCSource` of the scenario chooses the discount rate:

$$
wacc_f = \begin{cases}
w_c + adj_{coal,i(c)} & \text{Country*} \\
w_c + adj_{f,i(c)} & \text{Tech} \\
\max\left(w^{user}, w^{min}\right) & \text{User} \\
\max\left(w_{i(c)}, w^{min}\right) & \text{Income*} \\
\max\left(w^{s}_f, w^{min}\right) & \text{otherwise (studies)}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pw-wacc}

where $w_c$ is the country's real WACC (cost-of-capital data, 2022), $adj_{f,i}$ the technology premium of type $f$
for the country's income group $i(c)$, $w^{user}$ = `WACCUserGlobal` (default 0.075), $w_i$ the WACC of the income
group (HIC 0.075, UMIC 0.10, LMIC 0.125, LIC 0.15), $w^s_f$ the studies value and $w^{min}$ = `MinimumWACC` (0.01).
The default is Tech. Note that Country* adds the coal premium to every type. Code `wac`; the WACC is constant over
time ([WACC](#sec-pw-data-wacc)).

**Discounted lifetime.** The annuity factor turns a capital cost into a cost per year of life:

$$
dlf_f = \frac{1 - (1 + wacc_f)^{-N_f}}{1 - (1 + wacc_f)^{-1}} = \sum_{k=0}^{N_f - 1} (1 + wacc_f)^{-k}
$$ {#eq-pw-dlf}

where $N_f$ is the lifetime (years; the methodology's $lif_f$). Code `dlf`. Renewables' storage costs use
$dlf_{ren} = (dlf_{wnd} + dlf_{sol})/2$ (`dlfr`).

**Fuel per kWh.** $k_f = \theta_e/\nu_f$ GJ of fuel per kWh generated for types with a fuel price (coal, gas, oil,
biomass), 0 for the others (`kwh`). The CO2 intensity of generation is $e_f k_f$ tCO2 per kWh, with $e_f$ the
calibrated CO2 emission factor of the fuel in power (tCO2/GJ, @sec-emissions).

**Base-year capacity.** $cap_{f,t_0} = gen_{f,t_0}/cf_f$ (MW; `cap0`): the capacity consistent with base-year
generation at the capacity factor used.

**Investment rules, rates and factors.** The remaining settings of the scenario:

| Setting | Rule | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Investment permitted | `NewInv<type>`: Yes, No, Manual, or If Present* = Yes when the type has more than `InvPresentShare` (0.1%) of base-year capacity | `perm` |
| First year of investment | `NewInv<type>Year`; hydro from the base year when its base-year generation share is above `HydInvShare` (50%) | `start` |
| Permit of the year $\zeta_{f,t}$ | 1 if permitted and $t \ge$ first year, else 0 | `permit` |
| Scale-up rate $q_f$ | coal, gas, hydro: `MaxNonVREAsPCOfTotalGen` (0.05); oil, nuclear, other renewables, biomass: `MaxNonNucOreBioAsPCOfTotalGen` (0.02); wind and solar: by `MaxScaleUpRateCategory`, see below | `rate` |
| Wind and solar rate | CtryDefault*: the country's historical maximum (default 0.02; China and India 0.03); UserDefined: `MaxWindSolarScaleup` (0.05); Low 0.01, Medium* 0.02, High 0.03, Vhigh 0.04 | `scv`, `scat` |
| Retirement rate $r_f$ | $1/N_f$; hydro 0 if `HydroDoesntRetire` = Yes (default Yes) | `rr` |
| Early-retirement factor $f^{early}$ | `MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement` (0.8); in scenario 1 only if `EarlyRetirementInBaseline` = Yes (default Yes), else 0 | `erf` |
| Spot fuel prices | 1 if Settings `SpotPow` or the scenario's `UseSpotFuelPricesInEngineerModel` is Yes | `spot` |
| Capex decline scenario | `RenewableCostDeclineRate`: low, med (Medium*), hgh, vhg | `ctf` |
| Storage factors | $a_{st} \cdot 2 \cdot h_{100}$ and $a_{lt}\, u_{lt}$ ([Storage](#sec-pw-storage)) | `stm`, `ltu` |
| PPA share $\omega_t$ | [Dispatch](#sec-pw-ppa) | `ppa` |
| Renewable subsidy | [Renewable subsidies](#sec-pw-rns) | `rnsp`, `rns` |
| Rebate switch, electricity excise | [End-user prices](#sec-pw-excise) | `rbs`, `exs` |

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: inputs of the scenario (A0)"}
```
for f in types:
    low      = CFOverrideIfBelowWndSol if f in ('wnd', 'sol') else CFOverrideIfBelowFosOth
    cfu[f]   = cfa[f] if low < cfa[f] < CFOverrideIfAbove else cfs[f]
    nuu[f]   = nus[f] if nua[f] < MinimumThermalEfficiency else nua[f]     # nua = -1 without input
    wac[f]   = {'Country*': w_cty + adj['coa', inc], 'Tech': w_cty + adj[f, inc]}.get(WACCSource,
               max(WACCUserGlobal if WACCSource == 'User' else
                   w_income[inc] if WACCSource == 'Income*' else w_studies[f], MinimumWACC))
    dlf[f]   = (1 - (1 + wac[f]) ** -life[f]) / (1 - (1 + wac[f]) ** -1)
    kwh[f]   = GJperkWh / nuu[f] if f has a fuel price else 0
    cap0[f]  = gen0[f] / cfu[f]
for f in types:
    perm[f]  = NewInv[f] if NewInv[f] != 'If Present*' else ('Yes' if cap0[f] / sum(cap0) > 0.001 else 'No')
    start[f] = base_year if f == 'hyd' and shr0['hyd'] > 0.5 else NewInvYear[f]
    for t in years:
        permit[f,t] = 1 if perm[f] == 'Yes' and t >= start[f] else 0
    rate[f]  = MaxNonVRE if f in ('coa','nga','hyd') else (scv if f in ('wnd','sol') else MaxNonNucOreBio)
    rr[f]    = 0 if f == 'hyd' and HydroDoesntRetire == 'Yes' else 1 / life[f]
erf = MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement if scenario > 1 or EarlyRetirementInBaseline == 'Yes' else 0
```
:::

### Capital cost of new plants {#sec-pw-cax}

The capital cost of a new plant follows the capex time factor of its type:

$$
cax_{f,t} = cax^0_f\, \tau_{f,t}
$$ {#eq-pw-cax}

where $cax^0_f$ is the capital cost at time factor 1 (USD/kW) and $\tau_{f,t}$ the capex time factor of the decline
scenario (`tcf`): falling for wind and solar, 1 for coal, gas, oil and nuclear (medium scenario), and the scenario's
path for hydro, other renewables and biomass ([Capex time factors](#sec-pw-data-ctf)). Code `cax`.

### Amortised fixed costs of the existing stock {#sec-pw-fix}

The existing stock is a mix of plants built in different years at different capital costs. The model tracks the
average capital cost of the stock, and the average storage cost attached to it, as vintage averages: each year the
new plants of last year enter the average with their share in the stock.

$$
cax^{av}_{f,t} = cax^{av}_{f,t-1}\,(1 - \Phi_{f,t-1}) + cax_{f,t-1}\, \Phi_{f,t-1},
\qquad cax^{av}_{f,t_0} = cax_{f,t_0}
$$ {#eq-pw-caxav}

$$
sto^{av}_{f,t} = sto^{av}_{f,t-1}\,(1 - \Phi_{f,t-1}) + \ell_f\, msc_t\, \Phi_{f,t-1},
\qquad sto^{av}_{f,t_0} = \ell_f\, msc_{t_0}
$$ {#eq-pw-stoav}

where

- $cax^{av}_{f,t}$ is the weighted average capital cost of the stock (USD/kW; `caxav`);
- $sto^{av}_{f,t}$ the weighted average storage cost of the stock (USD/kWh; `stoav`);
- $\Phi_{f,t-1}$ the new investment of last year as a share of the stock after retirements (`phi`,
  @eq-pw-phi);
- $\ell_f$ the VRE flag (1 for wind, solar, other renewables);
- $msc_t$ the marginal storage cost of the current year (@eq-pw-msc). New vintages take the storage cost of the year
  they join the stock.

The amortised fixed cost per kWh then adds capital amortisation, average interest, decommissioning, storage and fixed
O&M:

$$
fix_{f,t} = \underbrace{\frac{cax^{av}_{f,t}}{cf_f\,H\,N_f}}_{\text{amortisation}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{\bar{s}\; cax^{av}_{f,t}\; wacc_f}{cf_f\,H}}_{\text{interest}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{dtc_f}{cf_f\,H\,N_f}}_{\text{decommissioning}}
+ sto^{av}_{f,t} + opf_f
$$ {#eq-pw-fix}

where

- $fix_{f,t}$ is the amortised fixed cost (USD/kWh; `fix`);
- $\bar{s} = 0.5$ is the average outstanding share of capital under straight-line repayment (`CapAvgShr`), so the
  interest term is the methodology's $0.5\, cax^{av}\, wacc/(cf \cdot 8760)$;
- $dtc_f$ the decommissioning (and, for nuclear, waste disposal) cost (USD/kW), not discounted;
- $opf_f$ the fixed O&M cost per kWh, fixed O&M per kW-year over $cf_f H$.

This is the methodology's $fix_B = acc + int + dec + sto + opf$
([section 3.4.1.6](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-3-cost-recovery-estimated-total-cost-of-generation)).

### Levelised fixed costs of new plants {#sec-pw-lfx}

A new plant's fixed costs are levelised over its discounted lifetime. The levelised fixed cost adds the capital cost,
decommissioning and a share of transmission capex, all annuitised, plus fixed O&M, the renewable subsidy and the
current marginal storage cost:

$$
fix^{fl}_{f,t} = \frac{cax_{f,t} + dtc_f + \kappa\, tcx_f}{cf_f\,H\,dlf_f} + opf_f + rns_{f,t} + \ell_f\, msc_t
$$ {#eq-pw-lfx}

where

- $fix^{fl}_{f,t}$ is the forward-looking levelised fixed cost (USD/kWh; `lfx`);
- $tcx_f$ the levelised transmission capex (USD/kW) and $\kappa$ = `TransmissionCostShare` the share of it included
  (default 1; legacy `IncludeTransmissionCostsInGenerationCostsPercent`);
- $rns_{f,t}$ the renewable subsidy per kWh, negative for a subsidy (@eq-pw-rns).

This is the methodology's $fix^{fl}$ with $sto = msc$, $pusRen = rns$ and the levelised transmission cost as the
$tcx$ term ([section 3.4.1.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-2-levelized-costs-of-generation-forward-looking)).
Because every component is constant in real terms over the plant's life, the levelised cost is the cost of one year
divided by one year's output: the methodology's constant-growth simplification
([3.4.1.5.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#lcoe-methodology-simplification)) with $\tau = 0$.

### Renewable subsidies {#sec-pw-rns}

A scenario can pay a subsidy per kWh to renewable generation. A base subsidy applies in every scenario; an additional
subsidy applies in policy scenarios from its own start year and phases out linearly:

$$
rns_t = -\left( s^{BL} + \mathbb{1}[o \ne B,\ t \ge T_s]\; s^{add} \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{t - T_s}{n_s}\right)\right) \iota_t
$$ {#eq-pw-rns}

$$
rns_{f,t} = h_f\, rns_t
$$ {#eq-pw-rnsf}

where

- $rns_t$ is the subsidy per kWh (USD/kWh, negative = subsidy; `rnsp`) and $rns_{f,t}$ by type (`rns`);
- $h_f$ is 1 for wind, solar, other renewables and biomass; for hydro 1 if `RenewableSubsidyHydro` = Yes, else 0;
  0 for the other types;
- $s^{BL}$ = `RenewableSubsidyBL` (default 0), $s^{add}$ = `RenSubsidyAddUSDkwh`, $T_s$ = `RenSubsidyAddStartYear`
  (default 2027), $n_s$ = `RenSubsidyAddPhaseoutYrs`;
- $\iota_t$ the CPI index: the inputs are nominal and are converted to real
  ([Reforms](#sec-pw-reforms)).

The subsidy enters the levelised fixed cost (investment), not the cost of the existing stock and not the end-user
price. Its fiscal cost is $rns_{f,t}$ times generation by type ([Power revenues](#sec-pw-revenues)). The equation list
has it in ([A4.7](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A4-7)).

### Current variable costs {#sec-pw-vc}

The variable cost is what a kWh costs to run: fuel, variable O&M, existing carbon pricing, and the new policies of
the scenario. It drives dispatch and, levelised, investment. Variable costs depend only on prices and policies, so they
are computed for all years before the year loop. The methodology describes them in
[section 3.4.1.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-1-current-variable-costs), with the fuel
price before new policies as in the corrected text
([corrections, DOC12](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/08_Corrections.html#corrections-of-2026-10-31)).

**Fuel price for power.** The price is the retail price before new policies of the type's price fuel, averaged over
the year and the four years before, within the model's years:

$$
\bar{p}_{f,t} = \frac{1}{t - \max(t_0, t - 4) + 1} \sum_{\tau = \max(t_0,\,t-4)}^{t} p_{f,\tau}
$$ {#eq-pw-fpp}

where $p_{f,t}$ is the retail price before new policies of the price fuel of type $f$ (USD/GJ; `fpn`; @sec-prices)
and $\bar{p}_{f,t}$ the price used (`fpp`). The average spans one year in 2022 and five from 2026. With spot prices
switched on, $\bar{p}_{f,t} = p_{f,t}$.

**Change in existing carbon pricing.** The price data already contain the existing carbon tax and ETS price of the
data year. A change in either after that year changes the cost per kWh:

$$
\Delta xcp_{f,t} = e_f\, k_f \left( XCT_{f,t}\,\phi^{ct}_t + XETS_{f,t}\,\phi^{ets}_t - XCP^0_f \right)
$$ {#eq-pw-xck}

where $XCT$ and $XETS$ are the existing carbon tax and ETS price of power and the type's fuel (USD/tCO2), weighted by
their coverage, $\phi^{ct}$, $\phi^{ets}$ their factors of the year, and $XCP^0_f$ the existing pricing embedded in the
price data (@sec-prices). Code `xck`; 0 for Egypt.

**Variable cost before new policies.**

$$
vc_{f,t} = vop_f + ffx_f + \bar{p}_{f,t}\, k_f + \Delta xcp_{f,t} + \mathbb{1}[f = \text{coal}]\; ipc_t
$$ {#eq-pw-vbc}

where $vop_f$ is variable O&M (USD/kWh), $ffx_f$ the fixed fuel cost (nuclear 0.004 USD/kWh, others 0), and $ipc_t$
the coal implicit cost ([Coal implicit cost](#sec-pw-coalic)). Code `vbc`. This is the methodology's
$vc = vop + p/\nu + ipc$.

**New policy cost per kWh.** The carbon tax, the ETS and the fuel price reform of the scenario, per kWh generated:

$$
ncp_{f,t} = e_f\, k_f \left( T_{pow,t}\; cov_{f,t} + A_{pow,t} \right) + \frac{F_{f,t}\, k_f}{u_f}
$$ {#eq-pw-ncp}

where

- $T_{pow,t}$ is the carbon tax rate of power (carbon price × sector coverage × (1 − ETS coverage), USD/tCO2; `ctr`)
  and $cov_{f,t}$ the fuel coverage of the carbon tax;
- $A_{pow,t}$ the ETS cost rate of power (tax-equivalent ETS price × ETS coverage × (1 − OBR share); `etr`);
- $F_{f,t}$ the new tax of the fuel price reform of the type's price fuel (price units; `ntxb`), $u_f$ GJ per price
  unit.

Code `xac`. The policy rates are those of @sec-model-overview; the same rates apply to the fuel blocks.

**Shadow price and rebate.** Feebates on power and the output-based part of an ETS act as a shadow price: they change
the choice between generation types without raising the average cost. The shadow price per kWh is

$$
sh_{f,t} = \Sigma_{pow,t}\; e_f\, k_f
$$ {#eq-pw-shk}

where $\Sigma_{pow,t}$ is the shadow price of power (feebate rate × share impacting efficiency + tax-equivalent ETS
price × ETS coverage × OBR share; `shpx`). The rebate returns it in proportion to base-year generation shares, per kWh
generated:

$$
reb_t = -\sum_f sh_{f,t}\; s_{f,t_0}, \qquad reb_{t_0} = 0
$$ {#eq-pw-reb}

where $s_{f,t_0}$ is the base-year generation share. Codes `shk`, `reb`.

**Total variable cost.** Dispatch uses

$$
tvc_{f,t} = vc_{f,t} + ncp_{f,t} + sh_{f,t} + reb_t
$$ {#eq-pw-tvc}

(USD/kWh; `tvc`). It is the methodology's $vc_P = vc_B + ncp$, plus the shadow price and its rebate.

**Levelised variable cost.** Investment needs the expected variable cost over a plant's life. The model takes the
discounted average of the total variable cost from the year to the end of the horizon:

$$
\overline{vc}_{f,t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau = t}^{T} \beta_{f,\tau}\, tvc_{f,\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = t}^{T} \beta_{f,\tau}},
\qquad \beta_{f,\tau} = (1 + wacc_f)^{-(\tau - t_0)}
$$ {#eq-pw-lvc}

(USD/kWh; `lvc`). It is computed backwards from $T$ with the sum of discount factors
$D_{f,t} = \sum_{\tau \ge t} \beta_{f,\tau}$ (`dsum`):

$$
\overline{vc}_{f,t} = \frac{\beta_{f,t}\, tvc_{f,t} + \left(D_{f,t} - \beta_{f,t}\right)\overline{vc}_{f,t+1}}{D_{f,t}}
$$ {#eq-pw-lvc-rec}

This is the methodology's levelised variable cost with the corrected discount factor
([corrections, DOC3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/08_Corrections.html#corrections-of-2026-10-31)); the capacity
factor of the methodology's weights is constant and cancels.

**Levelised investment cost.**

$$
tic_{f,t} = \max\left(fix^{fl}_{f,t} + \overline{vc}_{f,t},\ c_{min}\right)
$$ {#eq-pw-tic}

(USD/kWh; `tic`). The equation list has $vc$ and $tic$ as ([M4.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-3)) and the full variable
cost as ([A4.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A4-5)).

### Total costs {#sec-pw-total}

The cost-recovery generation cost of a type adds its amortised fixed cost and its variable cost before new policies:

$$
gnc_{f,t} = fix_{f,t} + vc_{f,t} - \mathbb{1}[f = \text{coal},\ \texttt{PwCoalICTariff} = \text{No}]\; ipc_t
$$ {#eq-pw-gnc}

The average generation cost weights it by generation shares, and the average new policy cost per kWh *consumed* adds
the losses and other uses between generation and consumption:

$$
gnc^{av}_t = \sum_f s_{f,t}\, gnc_{f,t},
\qquad
ncp^{av}_t = \frac{G_{t_0}}{D_{t_0}} \sum_f s_{f,t}\, ncp_{f,t}
$$ {#eq-pw-gncav}

where

- $gnc_{f,t}$ is the generation cost before new policies (USD/kWh; `gnc`), the methodology's $gnc_B = vc_B + fix$;
- $s_{f,t}$ the generation share of type $f$ ([Dispatch](#sec-pw-dispatch));
- $gnc^{av}_t$ the average generation cost (`gncav`);
- $ncp^{av}_t$ the average new policy cost per kWh consumed (`ccpav`), with $G_{t_0}/D_{t_0}$ base-year generation
  over base-year final demand (`gen_per_cons`, Egypt 1.266).

Carbon and other new policy costs are kept out of the average generation cost and added separately to end-user
prices. This lets a rebate be computed against them (methodology
[3.4.1.7](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#concept-4-end-user-prices)).

### Memos {#sec-pw-memos}

Memo rows report quantities that no other row reads.

| Memo | Equation | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Post-tax fuel cost per kWh | $\bar{p}_{f,t}\, k_f$ | `fce` |
| Carbon intensity (tCO2/kWh) | $e_f\, k_f$ | `cik` |
| Switching carbon price, gas over coal, investment (USD/tCO2) | $(tic_{gas} - tic_{coal}) / (cik_{coal} - cik_{gas})$ | `swi` |
| Switching carbon price, gas over coal, dispatch | $(tvc_{gas} - tvc_{coal}) / (cik_{coal} - cik_{gas})$ | `swd` |
| Current total cost | $\max(fix^{fl}_{f,t} + tvc_{f,t},\ c_{min})$ | `cur` |
| System cost | $(dtc_f + \kappa\,tcx_f)/(cf_f H dlf_f) + \ell_f\, msc_t + \mathbb{1}[\text{coal}]\, ipc_t$ | `sys` |
| Breakdown: capital | $cax_{f,t}/(cf_f H dlf_f)$ | `pcbcap` |
| Breakdown: O&M | $opf_f + vop_f$ | `pcbom` |
| Breakdown: fuel | $ffx_f + \bar{p}_{f,t} k_f + \Delta xcp_{f,t}$ | `pcbfu` |
| Breakdown: new carbon price | $ncp_{f,t}$ | `pcbcp` |
| Breakdown: renewable subsidy | $rns_{f,t}$ | `pcbrns` |
| Breakdown check | capital + O&M + fuel + system + carbon + subsidy − current total cost | `pcbchk` |
| Carbon tax of the scenario | $\tau_t\, \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]$ | `pcbct` |

A switching carbon price is the carbon price at which gas becomes as cheap as coal; a negative value means gas is
already cheaper. The breakdown check is zero unless the shadow price, the rebate or the floor $c_{min}$ act: they are not
columns of the breakdown (issue I142). The breakdown is computed for every year; legacy computes it for one
`CostBreakdownYear`. The equation list has it as ([A4.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A4-6)).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: generation costs"}
```
# before the year loop
for f in types:
    for t in years:
        cax[f,t]  = cax0[f] * tcf[f,t]
        fpn[f,t]  = rpb[price_fuel[f], t]                          # retail price before new policies
        fpp[f,t]  = fpn[f,t] if spot else mean(fpn[f, max(base_year, t-4) .. t])
        xck[f,t]  = ef[f] * kwh[f] * (xct[f,t] * xct_p[t] + xets[f,t] * xets_p[t] - xcp0[f])
        vbc[f,t]  = vop[f] + ffix[f] + fpp[f,t] * kwh[f] + xck[f,t] + (cic[t] if f == 'coa' else 0)
        xac[f,t]  = ef[f] * kwh[f] * (ctr['pow',t] * ctcov[fuel[f],t] + etr['pow',t]) + ntxb[price_fuel[f],t] * kwh[f] / gj[f]
        shk[f,t]  = shpx['pow',t] * ef[f] * kwh[f]
    for t in years:
        reb[t] = 0 if t == base_year else -sum(shk[f,t] * shr0[f] for f in types)
        tvc[f,t] = vbc[f,t] + xac[f,t] + shk[f,t] + reb[t]
    lvc_next = 0
    for t in reversed(years):                                       # backwards from 2041
        beta = (1 + wac[f]) ** (base_year - t)
        dsum[f,t] = beta + (dsum[f,t+1] if t < 2041 else 0)
        lvc[f,t]  = (beta * tvc[f,t] + (dsum[f,t] - beta) * lvc_next) / dsum[f,t]
        lvc_next  = lvc[f,t]

# in year t, after dispatch and storage (phi of t-1, msc of t)
for f in types:
    if t == base_year:
        caxav[f,t] = cax[f,t];  stoav[f,t] = vre_flag[f] * msc[t]
    else:
        caxav[f,t] = caxav[f,t-1] * (1 - phi[f,t-1]) + cax[f,t-1] * phi[f,t-1]
        stoav[f,t] = stoav[f,t-1] * (1 - phi[f,t-1]) + vre_flag[f] * msc[t] * phi[f,t-1]
    fix[f,t] = (caxav[f,t] * (1/life[f] + wac[f] * 0.5) + dtc[f]/life[f] + opfx[f]) / (cfu[f] * 8760) + stoav[f,t]
    lfx[f,t] = (cax[f,t] + dtc[f] + TransmissionCostShare * tcx[f]) / (cfu[f] * 8760 * dlf[f]) \
               + opfx[f] / (cfu[f] * 8760) + rns[f,t] + vre_flag[f] * msc[t]
    gnc[f,t] = fix[f,t] + vbc[f,t] - (cic[t] if f == 'coa' and PwCoalICTariff == 'No' else 0)
    tic[f,t] = max(lfx[f,t] + lvc[f,t], MinPostSubsidyPowerPrice)
gncav[t] = sum(shr[f,t] * gnc[f,t] for f in types)
ccpav[t] = sum(shr[f,t] * xac[f,t] for f in types) * gen_per_cons
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT: generation costs"}
**Simplifications (same numbers as legacy).**

| # | Legacy | Model | Same numbers? |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Five amortised-cost tables (B3 capital, B4 interest, B5 decommissioning, B6 storage, B7 fixed O&M) summed in B8 | One amortised fixed cost per type (@eq-pw-fix) | Yes (algebraically identical) |
| S2 | Six levelised tables (C1-C6) summed in C7; discount-factor tables A5, A6 | One levelised fixed cost per type (@eq-pw-lfx), discounted lifetime in closed form | Yes |
| S3 | Duplicates: A16 = B7 = C4 (fixed O&M), D7 = D8 (variable cost), E1 = E4 (investment cost), F2/F3 (fuel prices and fuel cost), E2 (cost before storage), E5 (breakdown memo) | Each quantity once | n/a |
| S6 | Coal implicit cost (D3) and the additional shadow price (D6) not built in the first build | Both built since ([Coal implicit cost](#sec-pw-coalic); @eq-pw-shk) | Yes |

**Fuel price for power (S5, L126, LD31).** Legacy averages the fuel price over $t-2 .. t+2$ (A18, rows 3155-3163),
which reads later years. The model averages $t-4 .. t$ within the scenario's own years (bug L126 fixed, user decision
2026-10-20); price changes reach power costs about two years later. The price row `fpn` holds this year's price, so the
average reads one row. Spot prices are a switch (Settings `SpotPow`, legacy dashboard option).

**Vintage averages.** The weighted average capex and storage cost of the stock match legacy exactly (B2, B6), with
last year's $\Phi$; new vintages take the current-year marginal storage cost.

**Rebate (L9, fixed).** Legacy adds the feebate rebate per kWh *consumed* to the cost per kWh *generated*. The model
returns it per kWh generated with fixed base-year shares (rows 3407-3409).

**Levelised variable cost (LD29).** The window runs to the last model year, 2041, as legacy; where the host cannot
evaluate the 2041 LAMBDA cell, the 2041 cost is last year's (`tvcx`). The legacy register also lists L127, "levelised
variable cost reads the variable cost to 2041".

**Existing carbon pricing (LD38).** The change in existing carbon pricing against the price data is a separate term
(`xck`); in legacy, existing pricing is part of the taxes of the power fuels.

**Cost memos (LD87, L222).** The memo tables E4 (current total cost), E5 (breakdown) and F1 (system cost) are computed
for every year; legacy computes the breakdown for `CostBreakdownYear`. The carbon tax of the breakdown reads the
block's own scenario (bug L222 fixed). F2-F4, F7 are `fce`, `cik`, `swi`, `swd`; F1, F5 and F6 are `sys`/`lfx`, `tic`
and `tvc`.

**Methodology.** The methodology's levelised cost discounted with $1 + wacc^{t - t_0}$ and lacked the sums over years;
both corrected (DOC3). The fuel price of the text and the equation now agree (DOC12). The units of $opf$ (USD/kWh) and
$dtc$ (USD/kW) are corrected (DOC13), and $opv$ is now $vop$ (DOC14). The methodology states that transmission costs
in % of capex are "not currently used"; the model includes them in the levelised cost at `TransmissionCostShare`
(default 1), as legacy does.
:::

## Dispatch {#sec-pw-dispatch}

Dispatch decides how much each plant generates this year. Plants that cannot or need not follow costs (renewables,
nuclear, oil, biomass) run at their capacity factor. Coal and gas, the flexible plants, cover the rest, shared by
their variable costs. Contracts that oblige coal and gas plants to run (PPAs) override part of that choice.

The methodology describes this in
[section 3.4.2.4.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#dispatch-decision), with the logit function of
[3.4.2.4.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#logit-function).

### Capacity of the year {#sec-pw-capacity-year}

Capacity is the stock of the previous year, less its retirements, plus its investment:

$$
cap_{f,t} = cap_{f,t-1} - ret_{f,t-1} + inv_{f,t-1}, \qquad cap_{f,t_0} = gen_{f,t_0}/cf_f
$$ {#eq-pw-cap}

where $cap_{f,t}$ is nameplate capacity (MW; `cap`), $ret$ retirement and $inv$ new nameplate investment (MW;
[Capacity and retirement](#sec-pw-capacity), [Investment](#sec-pw-investment)). Effective capacity, the generation the
capacity is expected to deliver, is

$$
cap^e_{f,t} = cf_f\, cap_{f,t}
$$ {#eq-pw-effcap}

(MW; `effcap`). This is the methodology's stock equation in capacity, with no sum over types
([corrections, DOC11](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/08_Corrections.html#corrections-of-2026-10-31)) and the equation
list's ([M4.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-5)).

### Fixed-output types and the coal and gas requirement {#sec-pw-fixed-output}

Wind, solar, hydro, other renewables, oil, nuclear and biomass generate their effective capacity:
$gen_{f,t} = cap^e_{f,t}$ for $f \notin CG$. Coal and gas must cover what is left of required generation:

$$
req^{cg}_t = \max\left(req_t - \sum_{f \notin CG} cap^e_{f,t},\ 0\right)
$$ {#eq-pw-reqcg}

(MWy; `reqcg`).

### Minimum runs and the logit share {#sec-pw-logit}

Each of coal and gas can generate at most its capacity at the maximum capacity factor:

$$
g^{max}_{f,t} = \mu_f\, cap_{f,t}, \qquad f \in CG
$$ {#eq-pw-gmax}

where $\mu_{coal}$ = `MaximumCoalCF` and $\mu_{gas}$ = `MaximumGasCF` (both 0.9 by default). Code `gmx`. Note that the
maximum applies to nameplate capacity: it lets coal and gas run above their base-year capacity factor when needed.

Each type first gets the minimum it must supply when the other runs at its maximum:

$$
g^{min}_{f,t} = \min\left(\max\left(req^{cg}_t - \sum_{j \in CG,\ j \ne f} g^{max}_{j,t},\ 0\right),\ g^{max}_{f,t}\right)
$$ {#eq-pw-gmin}

(`gmin`). The remainder is shared by a logit on relative variable costs:

$$
rem_t = \max\left(req^{cg}_t - \sum_{f \in CG} g^{min}_{f,t},\ 0\right)
$$ {#eq-pw-rem}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{f,t} &= \frac{e^{-K_{dispatch} H_{f,t}}}{\sum_{j \in CG} e^{-K_{dispatch} H_{j,t}}} \\
H_{f,t} &= \frac{\max(tvc_{f,t},\ c_{min})}{vc^{lc}_t},
\qquad vc^{lc}_t = \max\left(\min_{j \in CG} tvc_{j,t},\ c_{min}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pw-lambda}

where

- $rem_t$ is coal and gas generation left after the minima (MWy; `rem`);
- $\lambda_{f,t}$ the logit share of type $f$ (`lgd` is its weight $e^{-K H}$);
- $K_{dispatch}$ = `kDispatch` (default 2) the steepness of the logit;
- $H_{f,t}$ the variable cost relative to the cheapest of coal and gas, $vc^{lc}_t$ (`vcmin`).

The equation list has it as ([M4.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-4)). Generation before PPAs is the minimum plus the
logit share of the remainder, capped at the maximum:

$$
gen^{l}_{f,t} = \min\left(g^{max}_{f,t},\ g^{min}_{f,t} + \lambda_{f,t}\, rem_t\right), \qquad f \in CG
$$ {#eq-pw-glg}

(`glg`).

### Power purchase agreements {#sec-pw-ppa}

A share of coal and gas generation can be under power purchase agreements (PPAs): it runs at its capacity factor,
scaled to the need, whatever its cost. The PPA share of the year phases out linearly after a start year if the
scenario says so:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\omega_t &= \omega^0\, \phi^{ppa}_t \\
\phi^{ppa}_t &= \begin{cases}
\max\left(0,\ 1 - \max(0,\ t - T_p)/n_p\right) & \text{phase-out switch Yes or Yes*} \\
1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pw-ppa}

where $\phi^{ppa}_t$ is the phase-out factor, $\omega^0$ = `PPAProportionCoalGas` (default 0), $T_p$ = `YearPPACoalGas`, $n_p$ = `YearsToPhaseOutPPAs`,
and the switch is `PhaseOutCoalAndGasPPAsBaseline` in scenario 1 and `PhaseOutCoalAndGasPPAsPolicy` in the other
scenarios. Code `ppa`.

The PPA part runs at effective capacity scaled by the ratio of the coal and gas need to their effective capacity:

$$
\Omega_t = \begin{cases} \dfrac{req^{cg}_t}{\sum_{j \in CG} cap^e_{j,t}} & \sum_{j \in CG} cap^e_{j,t} > 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pw-omega}

$$
gen_{f,t} = (1 - \omega_t)\, gen^l_{f,t} + \omega_t\, \Omega_t\, cap^e_{f,t}, \qquad f \in CG
$$ {#eq-pw-gen}

where $\Omega_t$ is the downscaling factor (`ppr`) and $gen_{f,t}$ generation (MWy; `gen_mwy`). In the base year
generation is the data: $gen_{f,t_0}$ = base-year output of the energy balance. This is the methodology's
$\gamma = (1-\omega)\tilde\gamma + \omega\,\Omega\,(cap \cdot cf)$.

PPAs also protect coal plants from early retirement ([Early coal retirement](#sec-pw-early)).

### Generation shares, fuel use and CO2 {#sec-pw-fuel-use}

Total generation, shares, fuel use and CO2 follow:

$$
\begin{aligned}
G_t &= \sum_f gen_{f,t}, \qquad s_{f,t} = \frac{gen_{f,t}}{G_t} \\
FU_{f,t} &= \frac{8.76\; gen_{f,t}}{\theta_g\, \nu_f}, \qquad CO2_{f,t} = 0.041868\; FU_{f,t}\, EF_f
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pw-fu}

where

- $G_t$ is total generation (MWy; `gtot`) and $s_{f,t}$ the generation share (`shr`);
- $FU_{f,t}$ fuel use (primary energy) of generation (ktoe; `pe`): MWy × 8.76 gives GWh, divided by 11.63 GWh per
  ktoe and by the efficiency;
- $CO2_{f,t}$ CO2 from combustion (MtCO2; `co2`), with $EF_f$ the calibrated emission factor (tCO2/GJ; @sec-emissions).

Only coal, gas, oil and biomass enter the fuel totals (`pet`); nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables have
no fuel. The increase in total generation, $\Delta G_t = \max(0, G_t - G_{t-1})$ (0 in the base year; `dgen`), is used,
lagged, by early coal retirement.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: dispatch"}
```
for t in years:
    for f in types:
        cap[f,t]    = cap0[f] if t == base_year else cap[f,t-1] - ret[f,t-1] + nim[f,t-1]
        effcap[f,t] = cap[f,t] * cfu[f]
    reqcg[t] = max(req[t] - sum(effcap[f,t] for f not in CG), 0)
    vcmin[t] = max(min(tvc[f,t] for f in CG), MinPostSubsidyPowerPrice)
    for f in CG:
        gmx[f,t] = cap[f,t] * (MaximumCoalCF if f == 'coa' else MaximumGasCF)
    for f in CG:
        other    = sum(gmx[j,t] for j in CG if j != f)
        gmin[f,t] = min(max(reqcg[t] - other, 0), gmx[f,t])
    rem[t] = max(reqcg[t] - sum(gmin[f,t] for f in CG), 0)
    for f in CG:
        lgd[f,t] = exp(-kDispatch * max(tvc[f,t], MinPostSubsidyPowerPrice) / vcmin[t])
    for f in types:
        if f in CG:
            glg[f,t] = min(gmx[f,t], gmin[f,t] + rem[t] * lgd[f,t] / sum(lgd[j,t] for j in CG))
        else:
            glg[f,t] = effcap[f,t]
    cg_cap = sum(effcap[f,t] for f in CG)
    ppr[t] = 1 if cg_cap == 0 else reqcg[t] / cg_cap
    for f in types:
        if t == base_year:  gen[f,t] = gen0[f]
        elif f in CG:       gen[f,t] = glg[f,t] + ppa[t] * (effcap[f,t] * ppr[t] - glg[f,t])
        else:               gen[f,t] = glg[f,t]
    gtot[t] = sum(gen[f,t] for f in types)
    dgen[t] = 0 if t == base_year else max(0, gtot[t] - gtot[t-1])
    for f in types:
        shr[f,t] = gen[f,t] / gtot[t]
        pe[f,t]  = gen[f,t] * 8.76 / 11.63 / nuu[f]               # ktoe
        co2[f,t] = pe[f,t] * 0.041868 * ef[f]                      # MtCO2
```
:::

  `vcmin`, `rem`, `gmx`, `gmin`, `lgd`, `glg`, `ppr`, `gen_mwy`, `gtot`, `dgen`, `shr`, `pe`, `co2`; Formulas.md
  E391-E404, E408-E410; LAMBDAs `DISPATCH`, `LOGITW`). PPA row `ppa` in A0 (E303). Scenario inputs `MaximumCoalCF`,
  `MaximumGasCF`, `kDispatch`, `PPAProportionCoalGas`, `YearPPACoalGas`, `YearsToPhaseOutPPAs`,
  `PhaseOutCoalAndGasPPAsBaseline`, `PhaseOutCoalAndGasPPAsPolicy`.
- **CPAT Python:** `power.step()`, block "capacity and dispatch" (EQ-M4.4); `ppa` in `power.prepare()`.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT: dispatch"}
- **L11.** Legacy's dispatch formula has a stray reference; the model's has none.
- **Gas maximum (LD78).** Gas has its own maximum capacity factor `MaximumGasCF`; earlier prototype versions used
  `MaximumCoalCF` for both (legacy rows 3783-3786).
- **PPAs (LD75, issue I54).** As legacy (rows 3794-3805): the PPA part runs at its capacity factor scaled to the need.
  The phase-out switch accepts Yes or Yes*; legacy acts only on "Yes*", and its share to phase out is typed 1
  (issue I54). Legacy's scale-down row is not used.
- **Methodology.** The methodology's notation now writes the dispatch sums over one index with costs $c_f$ and the
  constant $K_{dispatch}$ (DOC14). It sets the maximum capacity factor at 90% "for coal and gas"; the model has one
  input per fuel.
:::

## Capacity, retirement and capacity needed {#sec-pw-capacity}

Each year part of the stock retires: plants reach the end of their lives, coal plants may follow a closure schedule,
and coal plants may close early when wind and solar are cheaper than running them. What retires, together with growth
in demand, sets how much new capacity is needed.

The methodology describes this in
[section 3.4.2.4.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#retirement-and-capacity-needed). The capacity
stock itself is @eq-pw-cap.

### Retirement {#sec-pw-retirement}

Retirement of a type is either its planned retirement (data) or a fixed share of its capacity; coal adds early
retirement; and nothing retires beyond the capacity there is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ret_{f,t} &= \min\left(b_{f,t} + \mathbb{1}[f = \text{coal}]\; early_t,\ cap_{f,t}\right) \\
b_{f,t} &= \begin{cases} pret_{f,t} & \text{planned retirement used for } f \\ r_f\, cap_{f,t} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pw-ret}

where

- $ret_{f,t}$ is retirement of nameplate capacity (MW; `ret`);
- $pret_{f,t}$ the planned retirement of the data, in nameplate MW per year (`pret`), used where the type's
  planned-retirement switch is Yes;
- $r_f = 1/N_f$ the retirement rate (0 for hydro if `HydroDoesntRetire` = Yes): retirement is exponential;
- $early_t$ early coal retirement (@eq-pw-early).

Effective retirement is $ret^e_{f,t} = cf_f\, ret_{f,t}$ (`rec`), so it is capped like the nameplate retirement. The
equation list has the rate-based form in ([M4.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-5)).

The planned-retirement data come from the coal plant tracker (plant-level retirement years, plants cancelled, shelved
or mothballed removed), averaged over five years ([Year paths](#sec-pw-data-paths)). The data exist for coal only; the
switch exists for every type. Coal is switched on where its averaged planned retirement over 2020-2030 is at least
0.1 MW per year (the data flag of the country).

### Early coal retirement {#sec-pw-early}

Coal plants may retire before the end of their lives when the variable cost of running them exceeds the full cost of
replacing them with new wind and solar. The model builds this in three steps: how much coal wind and solar could
replace this year, what share of it the costs favour, and the resulting nameplate retirement.

**Step 1: room for early retirement.** Wind and solar can grow by at most their scale-up limits
(@eq-pw-maxinv). Part of that growth is already needed for last year's increase in generation and to replace last
year's retirements of the other types. What is left is the room for replacing coal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
room_t &= \max\left(0,\ iv^{max}_{wnd,t} + iv^{max}_{sol,t} - \Delta G_{t-1} - \sum_{f \ne \text{coal}} ret^e_{f,t-1}\right) \\
room_{t_0} &= \max\left(0,\ iv^{max}_{wnd,t_0} + iv^{max}_{sol,t_0}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pw-room}

where

- $room_t$ is the room for early coal retirement (effective MW; `egrow`);
- $iv^{max}_{f,t}$ the maximum effective investment (scale-up limit) of wind and solar (@eq-pw-maxinv);
- $\Delta G_{t-1}$ the increase in total generation of last year (`dgen`);
- $ret^e_{f,t-1}$ last year's effective retirements of the types other than coal.

**Step 2: the share that costs favour.** A logit compares the coal variable cost with the levelised investment costs
of wind and solar, each relative to the lowest of the three:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s^{ec}_t &= \frac{e^{-K_i\, tvc_{coal,t}/c^{lo}_t}}
{e^{-K_i\, tvc_{coal,t}/c^{lo}_t} + e^{-K_i\, tic_{wnd,t}/c^{lo}_t} + e^{-K_i\, tic_{sol,t}/c^{lo}_t}} \\
c^{lo}_t &= \min\left(tvc_{coal,t},\ tic_{wnd,t},\ tic_{sol,t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pw-ecshr}

where

- $s^{ec}_t$ is the coal share of the logit (`ecshr`): high when running coal is cheap compared with building wind
  and solar;
- $K_i$ = `kInvestment` (default 2);
- $c^{lo}_t$ the lowest of the three costs (`ecmin`).

Equivalently, $s^{ec}_t = 1/\left(1 + e^{-K_i(tic_{wnd} - tvc_{coal})/c^{lo}} + e^{-K_i(tic_{sol} - tvc_{coal})/c^{lo}}\right)$,
the form of the workbook. The share replaced, $1 - s^{ec}_t$, is the methodology's $rep_{coa}$.

**Step 3: early retirement.** At most a fixed share $\bar{e}$ of coal's effective capacity can be replaced in a year.
The replaced effective capacity is converted to nameplate MW and scaled by the early-retirement factor; plants under
PPA do not retire early:

$$
early_t = \frac{\max\left(0,\ \min\left(\bar{e}\, cap^e_{coal,t},\ room_t\right)\left(1 - s^{ec}_t\right)\right)}{cf_{coal}}\;
f^{early}\,(1 - \omega_t)
$$ {#eq-pw-early}

where

- $early_t$ is cost-based early coal retirement (nameplate MW; `early`);
- $\bar{e}$ = 0.8 the maximum share of coal effective capacity (`EarlyMaxShare`);
- $cf_{coal}$ the coal capacity factor, which turns effective MW into nameplate MW;
- $f^{early}$ the early-retirement factor of the scenario (`erf`: `MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement`, default 0.8, and 0 in
  scenario 1 unless `EarlyRetirementInBaseline` = Yes);
- $\omega_t$ the PPA share (@eq-pw-ppa).

Early retirement enters coal retirement in @eq-pw-ret. The equation list has it as
([A4.9](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A4-9)).

### Capacity needed {#sec-pw-need}

Capacity bought in year $t$ comes online in $t+1$. The investment of year $t$ must therefore cover next year's
requirement. The model estimates it from this year's growth, so that no later year is read, and subtracts the
effective capacity left after this year's retirements:

$$
K^{after}_t = \sum_f cap^e_{f,t} - \sum_f ret^e_{f,t}
$$ {#eq-pw-kafter}

$$
need_t = \max\left(req_t\, \frac{req_t}{req_{t-1}} - K^{after}_t,\ 0\right)
$$ {#eq-pw-need}

where $K^{after}_t$ is effective capacity after this year's retirements (MW; `kafter`) and $need_t$ the effective
capacity investment needed (MW; `need`). In the base year the growth ratio is 1. Investment is sized on this need
([Investment](#sec-pw-investment)).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: retirement, early coal retirement and capacity needed"}
```
for t in years:
    maxinv = {f: rate[f] * sum(effcap[j,t] for j in types) * permit[f,t] for f in types}
    if t == base_year:
        egrow[t] = max(0, maxinv['wnd'] + maxinv['sol'])
    else:
        rec_other = sum(rec[f,t-1] for f in types if f != 'coa')
        egrow[t]  = max(0, maxinv['wnd'] + maxinv['sol'] - dgen[t-1] - rec_other)
    ecmin[t] = min(tvc['coa',t], tic['wnd',t], tic['sol',t])
    ecshr[t] = 1 / (1 + exp(-kInvestment * (tic['wnd',t] - tvc['coa',t]) / ecmin[t])
                      + exp(-kInvestment * (tic['sol',t] - tvc['coa',t]) / ecmin[t]))
    early[t] = max(0, min(effcap['coa',t] * 0.8, egrow[t]) * (1 - ecshr[t])) / cfu['coa'] * erf * (1 - ppa[t])
    for f in types:
        base_ret = pret[f,t] if planned_used[f] else cap[f,t] * rr[f]
        ret[f,t] = min(base_ret + (early[t] if f == 'coa' else 0), cap[f,t])
        rec[f,t] = ret[f,t] * cfu[f]
    kafter[t] = sum(effcap[f,t] for f in types) - sum(rec[f,t] for f in types)
    growth    = 1 if t == base_year else req[t] / req[t-1]
    need[t]   = max(req[t] * growth - kafter[t], 0)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 3, sub-table K: rows `pret`, `ret`, `rec` (K5, K6), `egrow`, `ecmin`, `ecshr`,
  `early` (K4), `kafter`, `need` (Formulas.md E411-E419). Constant `EarlyMaxShare` (0.8). Scenario inputs
  `kInvestment`, `MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement`, `EarlyRetirementInBaseline`, `HydroDoesntRetire`; planned retirement
  from `Inputs_ppath` (rows `pret|<type>`) and the switch from `Inputs_ptech`.
- **CPAT Python:** `power.step()`, block "retirement and investment" (EQ-M4.5, EQ-A4.9); `rr`, `erf`, `pret` in
  `power.prepare()`; planned retirement in `power_data.power_paths()` and `power_tech()` (`planned`).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT: retirement and capacity needed"}
- **L7 (fixed).** Legacy's early coal retirement mixes nameplate and effective capacity (rows 3975-3993). The model
  keeps them apart: the room and the cap are effective MW, divided by the coal capacity factor to give nameplate MW.
- **L8 (fixed).** Legacy does not cap effective coal retirement like the nameplate retirement (rows 4009-4019). The
  model derives effective retirement from the capped nameplate retirement.
- **Room (fixed).** The room for early retirement subtracts last year's *effective* retirements of the other types
  (legacy rows 3970-3974).
- **PPAs (LD75).** Plants under PPA do not retire early (legacy rows 3987, 3993).
- **Early-retirement factor.** As legacy F3993: `MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement`, and 0 in scenario 1 unless
  `EarlyRetirementInBaseline` = Yes. Legacy's maximum share 0.8 (J3975) is typed and not linked to
  `MaxCostBasedEarlyRetirement` (also 0.8); the model keeps it as the constant `EarlyMaxShare`.
- **L10 (fixed).** Legacy computes the capacity needed from last year's plan; the model from actual capacity after
  this year's retirements (row 4026).
- **L67 (fixed).** Legacy buys capacity for this year's requirement (row 4027-4028, labelled "Next Year Demand"),
  although it comes online next year. The model sizes it for next year's requirement, estimated with this year's
  growth so that no later year is read.
- **Planned retirement (LD26).** Every type has the switch and data rows; legacy offers it for coal only (K5).
  Legacy's "Use Data?" flag is `IF(AVERAGE(Z:AJ) < 0.1, "No", "Yes")` over the five-year averaged retirements of
  2020-2030 (Power F1750:F1857).
- **Methodology.** The methodology's early-retirement logit compares variable costs of coal, wind and solar; the
  model, as legacy, compares the coal variable cost with the levelised investment costs of wind and solar (the
  "total cost of wind and solar" of the methodology's text). The stock equation is in MW
  ([corrections, DOC11](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/08_Corrections.html#corrections-of-2026-10-31)).
:::
